identity.title: A transgenic pig model for human metabolic disorders defines the relationship between the colon pathological phenotype of metabolic disease, the microbiota and the intestinal barrier.

content.abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8(+) T cells, and CD79A(+) B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism. The humanized TG Bama pig model provides a clinically relevant large-animal platform for investigating the pathophysiology of metabolic disorder-associated colonic diseases and may facilitate the development and preclinical evaluation of therapeutic strategies targeting intestinal dysfunction.
